stops.campa: In 1985 a name is entered on the rolls of the Study of Mathematically Precocious Youth, the Johns Hopkins program that sits children years below the usual age in front of a college entrance examination and records what they do with it. He has already skipped three grades and been taught at home by his mother. The program does not teach him anything. What it produces is a number and a place on a national list of children like him.

stops.campa: The private project gets its first public description, an essay titled Urbit: Functional Programming from Scratch. Underneath sits Nock, an instruction set small enough to print on a page; above that a language, an operating function, and a namespace of identities named for galaxies, stars and planets. The premise is that general purpose computing has accumulated so much history that nobody can reason about it any more, and that the only fix is to start again from an axiom set one person can hold in mind.
